plan: Ten new items labelled easy or medium (abrupt and provisional WIC, octopus central idea, shade inference, solar-tilt data, dangling modifier, inverted agreement, addition transition, purpose synthesis, main purpose).

passages.title: A hurried ending
passages.text: Many reviewers found the novel's ending ______: after three hundred pages of mounting tension, the central conflict was resolved in a single, hurried paragraph.

passages.title: Trial policy
passages.text: The city's new parking policy was intended to be ______: it would remain in effect for only six months while officials studied its effects on traffic and local businesses.

passages.title: Tasting arms
passages.text: Each sucker on an octopus's arms contains thousands of chemical receptors, allowing the animal to taste what it touches. Because a large share of an octopus's neurons are located in its arms rather than in its central brain, an arm can respond to a promising taste, for example by grasping, before the brain has fully processed the signal.

passages.title: Shaded sidewalks
passages.text: A city planted trees along the north side of a long street but not along the south side. In summer, afternoon surface temperatures on the shaded north side were about 6°C lower than on the south side. Pedestrian counts showed about 40 percent more walkers on the north side in the afternoon, but no difference between the two sides in the early morning. These findings suggest that ______

passages.title: Panel tilt
passages.text:
An engineer measured the yearly energy output of identical solar panels mounted at different tilt angles.
Tilt angle | Yearly output (kWh)
0° | 410
20° | 480
40° | 455
60° | 380
The engineer concludes that output was highest at an intermediate tilt rather than at either the smallest or the largest angle tested.

passages.title: Ruins study
passages.text: Having studied the ruins for more than a decade, ______

passages.title: Canyon towers
passages.text: Along the canyon's northern rim ______ two stone towers that were built nearly a thousand years ago and are still largely intact.

passages.title: Recycled asphalt
passages.text: Recycled asphalt usually costs less than newly produced asphalt. ______ it requires less energy to make, because much of the material has already been processed.

passages.title: Raised dots
passages.text:
While researching a topic, a student has taken the following notes:
• Louis Braille was born in France in 1809.
• He lost his sight in an accident as a young child.
• At about age 15, he developed a writing system of raised dots.
• The system allowed blind people to read and write by touch.

passages.title: Replica display
passages.text: Light gradually fades the colors of old textiles. For this reason, a museum that owns a fragile seventeenth-century tapestry displays a carefully made replica in its galleries, keeping the original in a dark storage room where researchers may view it by appointment.

candidates.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
candidates.evidence: resolved in a single, hurried paragraph
candidates.explanation: An ending that resolves a long conflict in one hurried paragraph is sudden: "abrupt."

B.rationale: "Inevitable" means certain to happen; the complaint is about speed, not predictability.

C.rationale: "Subtle" means delicate or understated; a hurried one-paragraph resolution is not described as subtle.

D.rationale: "Lavish" means rich or extravagant, the opposite of a single hurried paragraph.

candidates.remember: The detail after the colon defines the blank.

candidates.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
candidates.evidence: it would remain in effect for only six months
candidates.explanation: A policy in effect only temporarily while it is studied is "provisional."

A.rationale: A policy lasting only six months is not permanent.

B.rationale: "Punitive" means meant to punish; nothing suggests punishment.

D.rationale: "Retroactive" means applying to past events; the policy applies for six months going forward.

hints: How long would the policy last?
candidates.remember: Match the word to the time limit the text describes.

candidates.stem: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?

choices.A: Octopuses have more chemical receptors than any other animal in the ocean.
choices.B: Octopus arms can taste and react somewhat independently of the brain.
choices.C: An octopus's central brain controls every movement its arms make.
choices.D: Octopuses rely mainly on vision to find food.

candidates.evidence: an arm can respond to a promising taste
candidates.explanation: The text describes the arms' taste receptors and explains that, because many neurons are in the arms, an arm can act on a taste before the brain fully processes it.

A.rationale: The text makes no comparison with other animals.

C.rationale: The text says an arm can respond before the brain has fully processed the signal.

D.rationale: The text discusses taste and touch, not vision.

hints: What two facts does the text connect?

strategy.explanation: Look for the choice that covers both sentences.

candidates.remember: A main idea covers the whole text without adding claims.

candidates.stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?

choices.A: the shade made walking on the north side more appealing mainly during the hottest part of the day.
choices.B: pedestrians preferred the north side at all times of day because of the trees' appearance.
choices.C: the trees lowered temperatures on the south side of the street as well.
choices.D: most pedestrians in the city walk only in the afternoon.

candidates.evidence: but no difference between the two sides in the early morning
candidates.explanation: Walkers favored the shaded side only in the afternoon, when it was much cooler, and not in the cool early morning, so the shade mattered mainly in the heat.

B.rationale: The counts showed no difference in the early morning.

C.rationale: The text compares the two sides; nothing suggests the south side cooled.

D.rationale: The text compares the two sides at each time; it says nothing about total numbers by time of day.

hints: When did walkers prefer the north side, and when did they not?

strategy.explanation: Eliminate choices that conflict with the morning result.

candidates.remember: Use every result, including the one that shows no difference.

candidates.stem: Which choice most effectively uses data from the table to support the engineer's conclusion?

choices.A: Output was 455 kWh at 40° and 380 kWh at 60°.
choices.B: Output at 0° was 410 kWh, which was higher than output at 60°.
choices.C: Output was 480 kWh at 20°, higher than at 0° (410 kWh) and at 60° (380 kWh).
choices.D: The panels produced a total of 1,725 kWh across all four angles.

candidates.evidence: output was highest at an intermediate tilt
candidates.explanation: The conclusion needs the peak at a middle angle compared with both extremes. C shows 20° beating both 0° and 60°.

A.rationale: This shows a decrease between two angles but does not show the peak.

B.rationale: This compares only the two extreme angles.

D.rationale: A total does not show which angle produced the most.

hints: What two comparisons does the conclusion need?

strategy.explanation: Identify the peak and the extremes in the table.

candidates.remember: Evidence for a peak must compare it with values on both sides.

candidates.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?

choices.A: the archaeologist proposed a new date for the city's founding.
choices.B: a new date for the city's founding was proposed by the archaeologist.
choices.C: the city's founding was given a new date by the archaeologist.
choices.D: the archaeologist's proposal gave the city's founding a new date.

candidates.evidence: Having studied the ruins for more than a decade
candidates.explanation: The introductory phrase must be followed by the person who studied the ruins: "the archaeologist."

B.rationale: The phrase would describe "a new date," which did not study anything.

C.rationale: The phrase would describe "the city's founding."

D.rationale: The phrase would describe "the archaeologist's proposal," not the archaeologist.

strategy.explanation: The word right after the comma must be the one doing the studying.

candidates.remember: An introductory modifier describes the noun right after the comma.

candidates.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
candidates.explanation: In this inverted sentence, the subject "two stone towers" follows the verb. It is plural, so the verb is "stand."

A.rationale: The subject, "two stone towers," comes after the verb and is plural.

B.rationale: "Standing" leaves the sentence without a main verb.

C.rationale: "Has" is singular and does not agree with "towers."

hints: Where is the subject of this sentence?

strategy.explanation: Rearrange: two stone towers ___ along the rim.

candidates.remember: In inverted sentences, find the subject after the verb.

candidates.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical transition?
candidates.explanation: The text lists two advantages of recycled asphalt: lower cost and lower energy use. "Moreover" adds the second advantage.

A.rationale: Requiring less energy is a second advantage, not a contrast with the first.

C.rationale: The second sentence adds to the first rather than replacing it.

D.rationale: Using less energy is not an example of costing less.

hints: Does the second sentence add a point or contrast with the first?
candidates.remember: Use addition transitions to join two points that support the same idea.

candidates.stem: The student wants to explain the purpose of Braille's writing system. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?

choices.A: Louis Braille, who was born in France in 1809, lost his sight as a young child.
choices.B: At about age 15, Louis Braille developed a writing system of raised dots.
choices.C: Born in 1809, Louis Braille developed his system while he was still a teenager.
choices.D: Braille's system of raised dots allowed blind people to read and write by touch.

candidates.evidence: The system allowed blind people to read and write by touch.
candidates.explanation: The purpose of the system is what it allowed people to do. Only D states that.

A.rationale: This gives biographical facts, not the system's purpose.

B.rationale: This says when the system was developed, not what it was for.

strategy.explanation: Look for the choice that answers "why."

candidates.remember: A purpose answers "what was it for?"

candidates.stem: Which choice best states the main purpose of the text?

choices.A: To explain why a museum shows a copy of a tapestry rather than the original
choices.B: To argue that museums should stop collecting fragile textiles
choices.C: To describe the process used to make replicas of old tapestries
choices.D: To criticize researchers for handling fragile objects

candidates.evidence: For this reason, a museum that owns a fragile seventeenth-century tapestry displays a carefully made replica
candidates.explanation: The text gives a cause (light fades textiles) and explains the museum's response (showing a replica, storing the original).

B.rationale: The text describes one museum's practice; it does not argue against collecting.

C.rationale: The text does not describe how the replica was made.

D.rationale: Researchers are allowed to view the original; no criticism is made.

strategy.explanation: State the text's purpose in your own words, then match.

candidates.remember: A main purpose describes what the whole text sets out to do.
